::: {.callout-note .legacy appearance="simple"}
This post is from the blog I kept as Preceptor in Mathematics at Harvard (2005–2008). It's kept here as an archive; some links are dead and references are dated.
:::

I just got back from the [Faculty Workshop on Technology In Teaching and Learning](http://isites.harvard.edu/icb/icb.do?keyword=k15850) sponsored by the Harvard Provost’s office. Some very rich food for thought.

- [Dan Moriarty](http://www.provost.harvard.edu/staff/moriarty.php), University Chief Information Officer: “Excellence in instructional techonology is becoming a *core competency* for faculty.” Once upon a time we played with the web and wondered if it would be relevant to teaching. Now that kind of debate seems silly.
- [Peter Bol](http://www.fas.harvard.edu/~ealc/people/pkbol.html), Professor of East Asian Languages and Civilizations: “Geotech, along with biotech and nanotech is one the biggest areas of growth in technology today.”
- Michael McCormick, Professor of Medieval History, “Today’s students are more visual that we ever were.” Images are the new texts, in a sense. Although he’s not ready to replace texts, it’s a good tool for us to bait-and-switch students into embracing the texts.
- Sid Verba, University Professor and Director of the Harvard University Library: “Many college students in the United States today have never been able to study the 19th century with the benefit of a book published in the 19th century.”
- Sameer Lakha, ‘09: “I don’t know how I use [facebook](http://www.facebook.com/) to enhance my student life. I just use it.”

The first part of the workshop was a presentation by Professor Bol about Geographic Information Services (GIS) and how they can be used in history courses. There is an unbelievable amount of data out there, indexed to places on the surface of the earth. Even a specialist in 7-17th century China can discover interesting patterns such as how the designation of certain capitals of Xi’an province as “thoroughfare capitals” led to the laying of railroads, which will form the basis of superhighways, and so on, through millennia of overlaid data. (There’s a nice [article from Harvard Magazine about GIS](http://www.harvardmagazine.com/on-line/110637.html)).

Professor McCormick then showed some of what he did in his [course on the fall of the Roman Empire](http://my.harvard.edu/icb/icb.do?keyword=k10321&pageid=icb.page35377). He used some of the GIS software to bring the roman empire to life, so that students “can really *feel* the heat of an sultry August afternoon in a roman seaport. He also created DVDs of his home videos and digital pictures from his visits to the places about which he was lecturing. He used this as a tool “to get students to come to class on time,” which by Harvard tradition is between 5 and 7 minutes past the hour. Finally, he and his TFs showed off a [baby GIS exploration tool](http://cga1.cga.harvard.edu/website/roman/roman/viewer.htm) they created on the web.

So I look at all this data, and I think, there’s math all over there. ![](http://i203.photobucket.com/albums/aa27/leingang_math/gis_sample.png){border="0" align="right"}Can’t we use this information to demonstrate what we’re teaching? The thing that I fear the most is the overload. For instance, I’d love to use it to teach regression in my [Math 20](http://www.courses.fas.harvard.edu/0906){target="_blank"} class, but is it too much data to handle without having to teach them how to use a piece of analytical software like Mathematica or Matlab as well?

As for the movies, that might be easier.  Visualizing mathematics has also grown in leaps and bounds with web technologies, all that’s needed is the elbow grease.  I want to learn more about [flash](/posts/pdf-and-flash/) so I can do more of this. 

At least on the aural level, this term I started getting to class a little bit earlier and playing jazz music from my IPod.  Just like in retail, the music gets students in the receptive mood, and it can start conversations as well.  It shouldn’t be too hard to set mathematical visualizations to great music.

The last of the faculty presentations was from Prof. Verba. He showed us some of the [Harvard Open Collections](http://ocp.hul.harvard.edu/): **[*Women Working, 1800-1930*](http://ocp.hul.harvard.edu/ww/)** and **[*Immigration to the United States, 1789-1930*](http://ocp.hul.harvard.edu/immigration/)**. He also showed the capabilities of the ever-growing [Google Books](http://books.google.com/) program that the Harvard Libraries are collaborating with.

Finally, there was a panel discussion on social computing in courses. Participating were

- [Prof. Michael Sandel](http://www.gov.harvard.edu/faculty/msandel/), who showed how he used blogs in his course to discuss bioethics
- [Prof. Rose Goldman](http://www.hsph.harvard.edu/faculty/rose-goldman/), who showed the blogs from her EH201 course in the Harvard School of Public Health
- [Prof. Andrew McAfee](http://dor.hbs.edu/fi_redirect.jhtml?facInfo=bio&facEmId=amcafee&loc=extn) ([blog](http://blog.hbs.edu/faculty/amcafee/)), who uses wikis in his Harvard Business School courses to organize the course content. Rather, he forces his students to use a wiki to organize the course and he grades them on it.
- Sameer and Rose Popkin ‘08, who did their facebook thing. They also mentioned [doodle](http://doodle.ch/) for scheduling and [Google Docs & Spreadsheets](http://docs.google.com/) for collaborative document editing.[]{.text_emph}

Until now I’ve been wary of using Facebook.  I created an account to find course assistants but I didn’t use it for much, and turned down friend requests from my students.  But it seems that using the “limited profile” feature I can separate my student friends from my actual NSFW friends.  So I’m looking forward to interacting with students there.

So in a few short hours I’ve got lots to think about over the summer and into the fall term.  Hopefully I’ll have the time to do some of them!
